name: VoiceAssistant-Eval
description: A comprehensive benchmark designed to assess AI assistants across listening, speaking, and viewing. It comprises 10,497 curated examples spanning 13 task categories, including natural sounds, music, spoken dialogue, multi-turn dialogue, role-play imitation, and heterogeneous images.
creator: Ke Wang, Houxing Ren, Zimu Lu, Mingjie Zhan, Hongsheng Li
rai:dataCollection: When collecting test data, the authors first extracted diverse visual and auditory inputs from source datasets, including natural sounds, music, dialogue, and images. The benchmark is organized into three subsets: Listening, Speaking, and Viewing. Listening source data were collected from 23 audio understanding datasets; Speaking source data came from RoleBench plus 22 datasets including 11 text datasets and 11 audio datasets; Viewing used MMMU as the source dataset. For role-play, they selected 100 distinct roles and collected three representative audio clips per role. To replace original text instructions, they synthesized spoken instructions using three TTS models, evaluated outputs with UTMOS, regenerated low-scoring clips, transcribed synthesized audio with Whisper, and retained recordings with the lowest word error rates.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw data come from source datasets. The paper states that diverse visual and auditory inputs were extracted from 37 datasets in one description, while Table 2 reports 47 source datasets. Listening uses 23 audio understanding datasets; Speaking uses RoleBench and 22 additional datasets; Viewing uses MMMU. Source datasets listed include, among others, VocalBench, AlpacaEval, MMSU, RoleBench, AdvBench, AIR-Bench, MEAD, BeaverTails-Eval, MT-Bench-101, VCTK, IFEval, MusicCaps, Common Voice, SD-Eval, Nsynth, BIG-Bench Hard, Clotho, SLURP, VoiceBench, MTG-Jamendo, JL Corpus, MELD, AudioCaps, AudioGrounding, CoVoST 2, LibriSpeech, VocalSound, VoxCeleb1, MUSIA-AVQA, FoR, SpeechInstructBench, IEMOCAP, FollowBench, SpokenWOZ, TUT2017, AVQA, CommonsenseQA, GSM8K, STORAL, Clotho-AQA, FMA, CochlScene, Fisher, MT Bench, RAVDESS, and MyST.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The authors converted collected text instructions into audio. For speech synthesis, they replaced image reference tokens with descriptive phrases, rewrote text to be more suitable for TTS using Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, and rephrased multiple-choice options for readability. They also reused 300 role audio clips as prompt audio to increase speaker diversity. Remaining examples were mapped to 13 task categories and balanced sampling was applied to equalize category representation.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The paper describes a multi-stage preprocessing and curation pipeline. First, text instructions were converted into audio. For synthesized speech, outputs were evaluated with UTMOS Strong and regenerated until the score surpassed 3.8; then Whisper-Large-v3 was used to transcribe synthesized audio and the sample with the lowest word error rate was selected. Data quality was improved through four stages: deduplication using lexical overlap and Levenshtein distance with manual review of suspected duplicates; validation removing incomplete or unsuitable instances such as corrupted images, silent audio, ill-posed prompts, and incorrect answers; categorization into 13 predefined task categories; and sampling to balance task ratios. Approximately 10% of candidates were discarded during validation.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The dataset consists of curated question-answer items with reference answers drawn from source datasets and curated through manual review. In the validation stage, curators reviewed each candidate item with its metadata, prompt, reference answer(s), and associated media, then assigned a Good or Bad verdict with optional notes. For role-play, the benchmark uses role profiles and question texts from RoleBench and evaluates role-specific speaking style and vocal timbre using collected role audio clips.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Suspected duplicates identified by lexical overlap and Levenshtein distance were manually reviewed and removed. During validation, curators checked media integrity, task well-posedness, and answer validity. Approximately 10% of candidates were discarded at this stage. The tool exported an audit log with item IDs, curator decisions, and timestamps; approved items were written to clean JSONL shards.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct, UTMOS Strong, Whisper-Large-v3, Whisper, Wespeaker, emotion2vec, gpt-oss-20b
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The authors state that they will release both the dataset and evaluation code used in the work, and that the data and open-source code are under an MIT license. They also state they will maintain a data governance process for auditing and removal and reserve the right to update assets if consent or licensing concerns arise.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The benchmark includes speaker voices and role-play voice imitation data. The paper explicitly discusses identifiable speakers, consent, provenance, anti-impersonation safeguards, privacy violations, and unequal performance across demographics. It also mentions user emotions with 7 emotion categories and includes five Chinese roles in the role-play task while other prompts and evaluations are in English.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper discusses that the benchmark can support development of next-generation multimodal AI assistants and applications in healthcare, education, smart homes, customer service, and automotive settings. It also highlights risks from role-play voice imitation, including identity spoofing, harassment, fraud, impersonation, privacy violations, and unequal performance across demographics. The authors propose safeguards such as consent gating, watermarking or traceability of synthetic audio, safety cards, and governance for auditing and removal.
rai:dataBiases: The paper states that the benchmark may carry biases from its source data and design choices. Questions and contexts are drawn from academic or synthetic sources, such as existing datasets and rewritten instructions, which might not reflect the full richness or fairness concerns of real deployments. The role-play subset uses a fixed set of 100 roles and associated style prompts, which may encode stereotypes or omit important user personas. The evaluation methodology also relies on automated measures and GPT-based scoring, which may introduce noise and bias and may favor certain phrasings or overlook nuanced errors.
rai:dataLimitations: The paper acknowledges several limitations. The dataset, though sizable, may still be limited in diversity. Although it includes five Chinese roles in the role-play task, all other prompts and evaluations are in English, so performance may not generalize to more diverse linguistic settings. The range of evaluated models is limited, with only one proprietary system included. The evaluation methodology relies on automated measures and GPT-based scoring, which may introduce noise and bias. The benchmark may carry biases from source data and design choices. There are gaps in task coverage and scenario realism, such as no video-audio integration or continuous audio-visual streaming tasks. The evaluation is offline and static and does not measure latency, partial utterances, barge-in, or error recovery. The dataset is not supposed to be used for training models for cheating, though the risk exists.
rai:dataUseCases: The intended use is evaluation and benchmarking of voice assistants across listening, speaking, and viewing, to facilitate future studies and transparent, longitudinal assessment of system capabilities. The paper states that researchers should use the dataset to better evaluate voice assistants. It is accompanied by evaluation code for result reproduction. The dataset is not supposed to be used for training models for cheating.
